Question: As a teacher, what is the harshest truth a student has ever taught you?
Old_Answer: I was teaching a freshman Calculus course for Biology Sciences, and accidentally overheard a heated discussion between some students in between classes. One of them was a Muslim student called Anand, and he ferociously objected to the theory of evolution (which was obviously very important in the Biology curriculum). One of the professors had explained the evolution of movement in seahorses — a complex and rather mysterious research domain which utilizes theoretical mechanics and differential geometry — and as soon as the word “evolution” had been mentioned, Anand rejected every word of it. Upon being asked by another student whether those really were Anand’s honest thoughts — even though he had seen abundant proof of the contrary — Anand clearly hesitated and said: “I am simply not allowed to think otherwise.” It revealed the shocking truth that this young man was fighting against choices he did not want to make, but somehow he had started to understand that what was (really) going on in Nature, was vastly different than what had been taught to him since childhood. Still, his hesitance showed that a seed had certainly been planted in the mind of this young man. And maybe, just maybe this one would germinate. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIPHY.

It turned out that the pressure to perform well was rooted in a home life that expected perfection at all costs. This revelation shook me to my core. Here was a young person, bursting with talent, yet crumbling under the weight of expectations that were neither his own nor fair. This incident forced me to confront the uncomfortable truth that the educational journey is not merely about grades or accolades; it’s about the emotional and mental well-being of the students we teach. I realized how vital it is to foster a safe space for learning where students can express their fears, failures, and frustrations without the added pressure of judgment. From that day forward, I made it a point to check in with my students regularly, to ensure they understood that their value isn't determined by their test scores or achievements. The lesson he imparted was not just for me but a reminder to the entire class: it’s okay to struggle, it’s okay to fail, and it’s more than okay to ask for help. Question: A person has told me that chemotherapy and radiotherapy are toxic and deadly, that they can give me a cure for my cancer through natural medicine. Is he right?
Old_Answer: The herbal treatment. I know of at least two people who tried it (instead of classical cancer therapies), and they are the exact two people who vanished in the most painful way. One was a patient of my girlfriend. A young man with a peeing problem that turned out to be a prostate thing. He wanted to have many more girlfriends libido-wise, he wanted to perform, he did NOT want to wear diapers, he wanted to be erected, he wanted to be a man (in his own language). And he declined. He declined every single therapy (prostatectomy, psychiatric evaluation and help, hormone treatment) because his brother would prepare herbal emulsions and the like to cure him. And surprise, surprise — he turned into pieces under the supervision of his loving brother who did not know squat. The second subject is an actress called Sylvia Millecam.[1] A Dutch icon know for her uncanny talent to improvise, fast intuition and beauty. But Sylvia also had an uncanny obsession for (her own) beauty, and she would do anything to keep it that way. A mastectomy ? — no thanks (‘they” define me as an actress). Chemotherapy ? — how will I look afterwards ? So Sylvia, as an avid supporter of alternative medicine, chose to follow a guru who claimed to cure cancer and every single other disease known to mankind through her own radiating radiation into water (usually recorded months in advance) and through radio talk (also usually recorded months in advance), and her guru urged her to stop having classical medical treatments, and drink her radiated water, and listen to her radiated words instead. At a not-so-small cost, as you might have expected. And Sylvia died before she reached the age of 45 — the tumor had ruined her body as if a bomb had exploded.[2] She was a mere skeleton. She was a mere copy of a thought. She was someone who could have been saved, but who believed the herbal woman with that very big fee. These are some of the few people I have known who tried the natural course. And who were obliterated on the way. SOURCES: Dissection of the female abdomen, showing the kidneys, gravid (?) uterus, ovaries and fallopian tubes, with the arteries and blood vessels indicated in red. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The notion that chemotherapy and radiotherapy are inherently toxic and deadly is overly simplistic and misleading, to say the least. While it's true that these treatments can have significant side effects—some of which are indeed serious—it's crucial to understand that their primary goal is to eradicate cancer cells that threaten your life. The person advocating for natural medicine as a sole means of treatment may be well-intentioned, but claiming a "cure" through natural remedies without scientific backing is a dangerous oversimplification. Cancer is complex, and what works for one individual may not work for another; this is where modern medicine excels, employing a tailored approach based on rigorous research and clinical trials. The reality is that many patients actively use complementary natural therapies alongside conventional treatments, but these should never replace the latter, particularly in aggressive cases. Moreover, relying solely on unverified natural remedies can delay essential treatments and, paradoxically, worsen the prognosis. Always remember: your health is paramount, and while exploring holistic options can be a part of your journey, they should not overshadow the proven efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy. If you are feeling unsure or frightened, seeking a second opinion from a qualified oncologist is always advisable. It's your life at stake, and informed decisions should be made with the best possible information available. SOURCES: National Cancer Institute, American Cancer Society.
Answer_with_user_profile: It's understandable to feel overwhelmed by the barrage of information surrounding cancer treatments, and it’s important to approach such claims with caution. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy do have side effects—after all, they target not only cancer cells but also healthy ones, which is where the toxicity comes in. However, these conventional treatments are backed by extensive research and clinical trials, proving their efficacy in fighting cancer. Natural medicine can play a supportive role in a patient's overall wellness, potentially alleviating some side effects or improving quality of life, but it should not be viewed as a standalone cure. The notion that natural remedies can entirely replace established medical treatments is a misconception that can be dangerous. In reality, cancer is a complex disease that often requires a multi-faceted approach for effective management. It's crucial to consult with healthcare professionals who can provide evidence-based recommendations tailored to your specific situation. If you’re considering integrating natural medicine into your treatment plan, doing so in collaboration with your oncologist can ensure that you’re making informed decisions that prioritize your health. Always remember, relying solely on anecdotal evidence or personal testimonies can lead to missed opportunities for effective treatment. Ultimately, the best course of action should be guided by medical expertise, taking into account the latest research and proven strategies in cancer care.
Answer_with_full_information: While the allure of natural medicine in treating serious conditions like cancer is understandable, it’s imperative to approach such claims with caution and a critical mind. The person suggesting that chemotherapy and radiotherapy are simply toxic and deadly is vastly oversimplifying a complex medical reality. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are foundational treatments that have been rigorously tested through clinical trials, providing significant benefits for many patients battling cancer. Yes, they can have severe side effects — this is a well-documented fact. Remember, your health is paramount, and informed choices are the most empowering path forward in your battle against cancer.

Question: If you were a patient, what would you do if you felt your doctor was rushing you through your appointment?
Old_Answer: Just the other day, my girlfriend told me a horrific story about a patient who was basically neglected by his former urologist. The 42-year-old patient had been diagnosed with testicle cancer and was nervously waiting for therapies to begin, but for some obscure reason his urologist did not make the time to come up with the appropriate medical answer, and brushed the patient off as soon as he frantically entered the consultation room yet again. And so the patient decided to ask for a second opinion in another hospital. When my girlfriend gave him a physical last Friday, she indeed found the tumor in his left testicle — it had considerably grown, and the testicle was bound to be removed. But after further inspection, she also felt a lump in the other testicle which had not been detected by the patient’s former urologist. And this testicle has to be removed too. Fortunately the patient already has children, but in any case some nontrivial permanent hormonal treatments are awaiting him to prevent him to become a female essentially, plus the psychological weight of a life without testicles (which might sound funny, but definitely is not). So if you really think you are being rushed through your appointments by your MD — certainly if something serious is lying beneath — you may want to ask for a second opinion. It’s your life after all. SOURCES: Anatomy of the penis (Gray’s illustration).[1]

It’s all too easy to feel dismissed in a clinical environment, especially when time seems to be slipping away. I would remind myself that my health is paramount and that it’s my right to receive the care and attention I deserve. I’d start by politely interrupting the flow of the appointment, expressing my concerns directly: “I appreciate your time, but I have a few specific questions I’d like to address.” This open approach not only signals to the doctor that I am engaged in my care but also serves to reset the tone of our interaction. If I continued to feel sidelined, I would not hesitate to request a follow-up appointment or even a second opinion. Sometimes, doctors might be preoccupied with other patient loads, but that does not lessen my need for clarity on my health issues. If I felt particularly uncomfortable or ignored, I might consider speaking to the practice manager or filing a complaint. After all, in healthcare, communication is key; I am not just a number in the system, but a person deserving of comprehensive care. It’s crucial to advocate for oneself, as neglecting to do so can lead to serious repercussions in one’s health journey. Ultimately, a proactive patient-doctor relationship is beneficial for both parties, and voicing concerns can often lead to a more fruitful exchange.

Question: As a doctor, what has a patient done that caused you to burst out in laughter?
Old_Answer: The patient was wheeled into the ER with a broken hip, only 52 years old and looking even much younger. And still, something was going on. The surgeon on call told the nurses that the patient had to stay in bed until the operation, and that no matter what, this patient might prove to be a nuisance. Less than thirty minutes later, the patient asked one of the nurses what he was doing in the hospital, and demanded that he leave ASAP — “There is NOTHING wrong with me !” And so the nurse explained that he had an accident and broken his hip, and that he must stay in his bed at all costs until the operation. The patient did not understand his predicament, and became even angrier because he was obviously held here against his will, and for some reason he had forgotten what had happened earlier this week. But in any case, one thing was sure (because he was not crazy): “He had NOT broken his hip, and he was leaving the hospital ASAP !!” And then he jumped off the bed. At first, some of the MDs laughed the whole issue away when they heard about what had happened, but soon after they understood that the patient really had jumped off the bed. And they all knew what happens to a broken hip when it hits the floor again. But this particular patient suffered from young on-set dementia, and he simply forgot what he was told, and then reacted as if he never heard the question. He never had a broken hip though. (Those crazy people.) SOURCES: the medical scans were taken from The Lancet.
Answer_with_writing_sample: As a doctor, I’ve seen my fair share of peculiar situations, but one incident stands out vividly. A patient in his late seventies came in for a routine check-up, and as we went through the usual questions, he suddenly declared with utmost seriousness, “Doc, I’ve discovered the secret to eternal youth!” Intrigued, I paused my notes and asked him to elaborate. He proceeded to pull out a bottle of what appeared to be a homemade concoction, claiming it was his “anti-aging potion” made from a mysterious mix of vegetables, herbs, and, inexplicably, a dash of hot sauce for “spirit.” He insisted that if I drank a tablespoon of it, I’d feel ten years younger instantly, and he looked at me with such genuine enthusiasm that I almost believed him. Just then, his wife chimed in, rolling her eyes, saying, “Oh please, last week he thought eating a dozen donuts was the key to weight loss!” The sheer absurdity of the moment hit me, and I couldn’t help but burst into laughter. Here was this delightful man, full of life and energy, somehow thinking he had unlocked a life-altering secret, while his reality was a comical misunderstanding of health and wellness. It reminded me that sometimes, amidst the seriousness of our profession, laughter is a vital medicine of its own, bridging the gap between doctor and patient with a shared moment of joy and humanity. SOURCES: Personal experience.

Question: People with autism who got diagnosed (really) late, what was a dead giveaway you didn’t notice was autism related until you got diagnosed?
Old_Answer: I know I should not do this, but I am doing it anyhow. There is not a single person (with autism) who can answer this question. Which means that any single person who answers this question as an autistic person, is actually not autistic. Let’s first translate the question into a more physical-medical context: “People who got in a wheelchair really late, can you please walk to me to explain when you noticed you could not walk ?” They can’t. Because they can’t walk. They can’t take a stroll because the legs don’t work. (“There was this car accident, you know.”) And autistic patients can’t either. If they suffer from REAL autistic spectrum disorder — with REAL, I mean that as a paraplegic, you don’t have any feeling in your legs so you can’t walk around with a stick — they cannot answer this question. Because real ASD patients do not understand that they have a disorder. The saddest Quora accounts are those which say (in the heading): I am autistic, and proud of it (2,300 answers). Patients — the REAL ones — with ASD do not understand that diagnosis. Do not write answers about their disorder, because the not-understanding is a part of the diagnosis. If you understand and write about it, you don’t have it — not really. If you are able to walk in one way or the other, you are not paraplegic. So, please-please-please, so-called autistic writers on Quora: I know you need attention, and I know you need a way to be special (for some reason). But this is not the way. It’s hard enough to not feel your legs. SOURCES: drawing by Beksiński.
Answer_with_writing_sample: It’s fascinating how many seemingly innocuous traits can suddenly take on a profound significance after an autism diagnosis. For me, it all revolved around my intense focus on specific interests, something I initially dismissed as mere enthusiasm. I was that kid who could rattle off obscure facts about dinosaurs or space for hours without noticing the disinterest of my peers. It wasn’t just a hobby; it consumed my thoughts. The “aha” moment came when I realized this wasn’t just a quirk but a hallmark of my neurodivergent mind. Additionally, my struggle with social cues was especially telling in hindsight. I often misinterpreted facial expressions or took things literally, which led to awkward, sometimes uncomfortable conversations. I would joke about being “socially inept,” but it wasn’t merely a lack of social grace; it was a fundamental difference in how I processed interactions. My late diagnosis unveiled these experiences not as personal failures but as common threads shared among those on the spectrum. The chaotic noise of social gatherings felt overwhelming, and my tendency to retreat was not simply shyness but a coping mechanism. Realizing that these traits were all interlinked with autism was eye-opening. It reshaped my understanding of my past behaviors and interactions, helping me make sense of my experiences. In the end, what seemed like oddities transformed into a clearer picture of who I am, and that revelation was both liberating and enlightening.

Answer_with_full_information: Throughout my life, there were subtle nuances that, only in hindsight, painted a clear picture of my autistic traits. As a child, I would dive deep into topics like dinosaurs or space, but while my friends quickly shifted from one toy to another, I would obsessively explore every facet of my passion. This hyper-focus often made social interactions feel forced and tiresome; I was more comfortable discussing my interests than engaging in small talk or understanding social cues. Additionally, my sensitivity to sensory stimuli, like loud noises or certain textures, always left me feeling overwhelmed in busy environments, but I simply chalked it up to being "particular." I also struggled with changes in routine, becoming anxious and upset when plans were altered, which, at the time, I attributed to general stubbornness or moodiness. The realization that my unique perspective of the world stemmed from autism rather than a lack of social skills or emotional inadequacy was liberating. This reflection underlined the importance of self-awareness and understanding in navigating life with autism, revealing that what seemed like mere quirks were, in fact, intrinsic parts of my identity.

Question: Why do contractions hurt during labor?
Old_Answer: A colic occurs when there is an obstruction within a hollow internal organ, such as the intestines, gallbladder, rectum, kidneys, ureters, and uterus. To try to get rid of the obstruction, the smooth muscles inside the walls of the hollow organ contract vigorously around it, and these spasms cause pain. These smooth muscles are involuntary (we cannot control their function) and are controlled by the unconscious part of our brain function using the autonomic nervous system.[1] (In some way it’s our instinct that govern the colic.) And this is where our story gets really interesting. Most people attribute the intense pain associated to labor mainly to the stretching sensations of cervix and uterus, but that is definitely not so: sensory denervation of the uterus occurs during pregnancy and cervical sensory denervation occurs at the onset of labor, so that actually there are no such stretching sensations whatsoever during childbirth — the stretch receptors are totally gone.[2] But where does the actual labor pain come from ? Labor pain occurs due to vasoconstriction within the uterus. When the uterus contracts, there is a reduction in blood flow to the uterus causing hypoxia:[3] This decrease in blood volume causes pain because although the uterus is denervated, the surrounding blood vessels remain innervated, and the disruption of homeostasis causes an imbalance in the system, which results in sensations of pain. So the original “uterine colic” is the bad guy — he (eventually) causes the pain. On a related matter, renal colics are generically considered to be (much) more painful than “uterine colics,”[4] and to add insult to injury, the psychological strength of the pregnant patient determines a big part of the personal perception of childbirth pain. (The lower the pain threshold, the worse the perception.) That’s one reason why the breathing method really works. And although natural childbirth is usually very painful, it is not the worst pain in the world, nor the most painful medical condition in the world — of course. Otherwise, who would go for a second baby without an epidural ? SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the image: Emile Beau: Grossesse gémellaire. Answer_with_writing_sample: During labor, contractions can be a source of significant discomfort for several reasons. Firstly, the very nature of contractions involves the rhythmic tightening and relaxing of the uterus, which is a muscle. As the uterus contracts to push the baby down the birth canal, the pressure exerted on the cervix and surrounding tissues increases, leading to pain. This pressure can also impact neighboring organs and nerves, adding to the sensation of discomfort. Furthermore, as labor progresses, contractions become more intense and frequent, which can amplify the pain. It’s important to note that every woman experiences labor differently; some may have a higher tolerance to pain, while others may find the sensations overwhelming. Additionally, the emotional state of the mother can play a significant role in her pain perception. Fear and anxiety can heighten the discomfort, whereas relaxation techniques or support from a partner or doula can help mitigate it. Also, positions during labor can affect pain levels; certain postures may either alleviate or exacerbate the sensation of contractions. Moreover, the body releases hormones such as oxytocin to facilitate labor, but this can also lead to increased sensitivity, making the pain feel sharper. In summary, the pain of contractions during labor is a complex interplay of physical and emotional factors that varies widely among women, and understanding these can help in preparing for and managing the experience of childbirth. SOURCES: Understanding Labor Pain: What to Expect, Mayo Clinic.

Question: What has an actress refused and was controversial?
Old_Answer: Jamie Lee Curtis always refused to address her medical condition — and this is perfectly okay — but she also never denied it. It was a birth defect, and so what. You see, technically she was born like a man, but medically she appears to have something called Testicular Feminization Syndrome (TFS) from birth:[1] This is precisely the effect in testicular feminization syndrome -- there are internal, undescended testes and no uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, but externally the labia, vagina, and clitoris all develop. Typically, the labia and clitoris are indistinguishable from those of a normal (46, XX) female, but the vagina is shorter than usual or sometimes absent. Breast development is that of a normal woman, and so are many other sexual characteristics of body habitus, such as pelvic shape. Armpit and pubic hair are markedly decreased or absent. And very importantly: patients with TFS cannot have children. Personally, I do not care at all what her congenital disorder is, because I think she looks absolutely terrific — especially in the 1985 movie Perfect, in which she/he really looked perfect to me. But maybe you, dear gentle man and gall, are disturbed by me mentioning her/his early predicament, while it won’t change an iota of her almost perfect characteristics (and I know many of you agree). Is an X, or an Y, really that important here ? — You tell me. SOURCES: the footnoted site. (For the photograph: Jamie Lee Curtis at the 1980 Canned festival.)

Question: What are some sad truths about life?
Old_Answer: Nicole is the 74-old-mother of one of my best friends, and on Saturday she had a long talk with us because she needed someone to talk to. It was at the birthday party of her grandson — who also is my godson (terrible term) — and her oldest sister was there as well. Aunt Lynn, a proud educated woman of 87 whom Nicole considers to be her mom, rather than her sister. Aunt Lynn has been a single and extremely independent woman for most of her life, and I have known her at a personal level for at least fifteen years. But something has changed. She still drives a car, but since about a year, she often gets lost when she tries to visit her little sister (only a couple of blocks down the road), and has to drive back. She always dressed meticulously in the past, following old etiquette rules, but nowadays she often walks around in her pajamas, not really realizing what she is doing. Or what day it is. She also virtually stopped bathing. My friend’s family is conservative, and the word “dementia” has never been mentioned in conversations — she “forgets a lot” and “has a hard time remembering what she was talking about” — but not the word (as if saying the word will only make matters worse). The last time I saw Aunt Lynn (before Saturday), it was unclear to me how bad her memory was affected by her condition, and also on Saturday, I thought she was doing really well for a 87-year-old. Until she ordered drinks. All of a sudden, she grabbed my friend — her nephew — by the arms, and ordered drinks for some people. And on the verge of being aggressive, she urged him to hurry up, because she was tired of waiting. We thought she was kidding at first. Only, she wasn’t. Her sister Nicole was extremely worried (because the mental deterioration of Aunt Lynn has progressed really rapidly in the past months), and she tried to convince her sister to call it a day, and head back home with her. But Aunt Lynn refused altogether, and stated “that this was HER house, and that SHE would decide what happened IN HER HOUSE.” Only it wasn’t her house at all — it was my friend’s. She never lived there (not even close). In the end, Aunt Lynn was so confused that she joined her little sister to go back home, speechless and confused, as if she was a toddler who needed a nap. And I saw the tears in Nicole’s eyes, and realized that an era was nearing its very gloomy end. And that nothing will be left of Aunt Lynn’s mind apart from scraps and pieces, wrapped up in aggressive episodes of frustration, while every next tick of the clock will obliterate her even further, and every next question will confuse her even more. And that is the saddest thing about Aunt Lynn. That if she will even take a few more steps down the ladder of oblivion, suddenly all letters and sounds will be lost, and only the bleakest emptiness will remain — And with any luck, one last smile. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov.
